chapter_sections.label: Definition:
chapter_sections.text:
Crop Production and Management refers to all the agricultural
activities and practices carried out by farmers to grow plants
of the same kind on a large scale in order to provide food for
a growing population.

chapter_sections.label: Key Points:
points: Plants of the same kind cultivated at one place on a large
scale are called a CROP.
Crops are classified based on season: KHARIF and RABI crops.
Providing food to a large population requires regular
production, proper management and distribution.
Agricultural practices include preparation of soil, sowing,
adding manure and fertilisers, irrigation, protection from
weeds, harvesting and storage.

items.question: Name the two broad types of crops grown in India
items.answer:
The two broad types of crops in India are:
1. KHARIF CROPS - grown in the rainy season (June to
September). Examples: paddy, maize, soyabean, groundnut,
cotton.
2. RABI CROPS - grown in the winter season (October to March).
Examples: wheat, gram, pea, mustard, linseed.

items.question: List the basic agricultural practices involved in
items.answer:
The basic agricultural practices involved in crop production
are:
(i) Preparation of soil - tilling and loosening of soil
(ii) Sowing - placing seeds in the soil at proper depth and
distance
(iii) Adding manure and fertilisers - replenishing nutrients
in the soil
(iv) Irrigation - supplying water to crops at regular
intervals
(v) Protection from weeds - removing unwanted plants
(vi) Harvesting - cutting the mature crop
(vii) Storage - keeping the harvested grains safely
These practices together ensure good crop yield.

items.question: Why is it important to provide food to a large
items.answer:
India has a large and growing population. All living organisms
including humans require food for energy to carry out body
functions such as digestion, respiration and excretion.
We get our food from plants, animals or both.
To provide food to a large number of people, food has to be
produced on a large scale. Crop production plays a key role
because:
- It ensures regular production of food items
- It allows proper management of available land and resources
- It ensures proper distribution of food to the population
Without organised crop production, it would be impossible to
feed billions of people.

items.question: Explain why crops are classified based on seasons.
items.answer:
India is a vast country with varying climatic conditions like
temperature, humidity and rainfall from one region to another.
Different crops require different climatic conditions to grow
well. Because of this variation in climate across seasons,
crops are classified based on the season in which they grow.

KHARIF CROPS:
- Grown in the rainy season (June to September)
- Require a lot of water and warm weather
- Examples: Paddy (rice) and Maize
- Paddy requires a lot of water, so it is grown only in the
rainy season
- Other examples: soyabean, groundnut, cotton

RABI CROPS:
- Grown in the winter season (October to March)
- Require cool weather during growth and warm weather to ripen
- Examples: Wheat and Gram (chickpea)
- Other examples: pea, mustard, linseed

Besides these, pulses and vegetables are also grown during
summer at many places.

This classification helps farmers choose the right crop for
the right season, ensuring better yield and efficient use of
land and resources.

items.question: What is animal husbandry? Why is it considered
items.answer:
ANIMAL HUSBANDRY is the practice of rearing animals at home
or in farms on a large scale and providing them with proper
food, shelter and care.

Just like crop production involves a series of steps such as
selection of seeds, sowing, manuring, irrigation and
harvesting, animal husbandry also involves:
- Selecting the right animals to rear
- Providing proper and nutritious food to animals
- Ensuring adequate shelter and clean living conditions
- Taking care of animal health and hygiene
- Managing the produce obtained from animals (milk, eggs,
wool, meat, etc.)

Animals like cows, buffaloes, she-goat, she-camel provide
milk. Fish provide fish and fish products including cod liver
oil which is rich in Vitamin D.

Animal husbandry is considered similar to crop production
because both are large-scale organised activities for
producing food, both require systematic management, proper
care and resources, and both are essential parts of
agriculture.

items.question: Describe the complete journey of crop production
items.answer:
Crop production involves a series of steps that farmers follow
carefully to get a good yield. The complete journey is as
follows:

STEP 1 - PREPARATION OF SOIL:
The soil is turned and loosened using a plough (tilling or
ploughing). This allows roots to breathe, helps earthworms
and microbes to grow, brings nutrient-rich soil to the top,
and helps water to penetrate deep. Tools used: plough, hoe,
cultivator.

STEP 2 - SOWING:
Good quality, healthy seeds are selected (damaged seeds
float on water and are rejected). Seeds are sown at proper
depth and distance using traditional tools (funnel-shaped)
or seed drills. Proper spacing ensures each plant gets
sufficient sunlight, nutrients and water.

STEP 3 - ADDING MANURE AND FERTILISERS:
Soil nutrients get depleted with continuous cultivation.
Manure (organic - from decomposed plant/animal waste) and
fertilisers (chemical - urea, NPK, super phosphate) are
added to replenish nutrients. Crop rotation also helps
replenish nitrogen in the soil.

STEP 4 - IRRIGATION:
Water is supplied to crops at regular intervals. Sources
include wells, tubewells, ponds, lakes, rivers, dams and
canals. Modern methods like sprinkler system and drip system
conserve water. Drip system is best as water falls drop by
drop near the roots - no wastage.

STEP 5 - PROTECTION FROM WEEDS:
Unwanted plants called weeds grow alongside crops and compete
for water, nutrients, space and light. They are removed by
tilling, manually using a khurpi, or by spraying chemical
weedicides like 2,4-D. Weeding should be done before weeds
produce flowers and seeds.

STEP 6 - HARVESTING:
After 3-4 months the crop matures and is cut. This cutting is
called harvesting. It is done manually using a sickle or by
a machine called a harvester/combine. The grain is separated
from chaff by threshing (using a combine) or winnowing.

STEP 7 - STORAGE:
Harvested grains are dried in the sun to reduce moisture.
They are stored in jute bags (small scale), or in silos and
granaries (large scale) protected from pests like rats,
insects and microorganisms. Dried neem leaves are used at
home for storing food grains.

Each step is important: skipping or doing poorly at any one
step can result in loss of crop, poor yield or damaged grain.
Together, these steps ensure food security for the entire
population.

items.question: Why do we need to eat food? Where do we get our
items.answer:
We need to eat food because:
- All living organisms require energy to carry out their body
functions such as digestion, respiration and excretion.
- This energy comes from the food we eat.
- Without food, organisms cannot survive.

We get our food from:
- PLANTS: Rice, wheat, vegetables, fruits, pulses - we get
these directly from plants.
- ANIMALS: Milk from cows/buffaloes, eggs from hens, meat
from animals, fish from water bodies.
- BOTH: Many food items come from plant and animal sources.

Plants are special because they can make their own food
through photosynthesis. Animals including humans cannot make
their own food and depend on plants or other animals.

items.question: How are crops classified in India? Give reason
items.answer:
In India, crops are broadly classified into two types based
on the season in which they are grown:

1. KHARIF CROPS:
- Grown in the rainy season (June to September)
- India's rainy season provides the required water and
warmth for these crops
- Examples: Paddy, Maize, Soyabean, Groundnut, Cotton

2. RABI CROPS:
- Grown in the winter season (October to March)
- Cool weather during growth and warm weather to ripen
suits these crops
- Examples: Wheat, Gram, Pea, Mustard, Linseed

REASON FOR CLASSIFICATION:
India is a vast country with varying climatic conditions of
temperature, humidity and rainfall. Different crops require
different climatic conditions to grow well. Classifying crops
by season helps farmers choose the right crop for each season
to get good yield.

items.question: What is agriculture? Trace the history of how
items.answer:
AGRICULTURE is the science and practice of cultivating land,
growing crops and rearing animals for food and other products.

HISTORY OF AGRICULTURE:
- Until about 10,000 B.C.E., human beings were NOMADIC.
- They wandered in groups from place to place in search of
food and shelter.
- They ate raw fruits and vegetables and hunted animals for
food.
- Gradually, they learned to cultivate land and produce crops
like rice and wheat.
- This marked the BIRTH OF AGRICULTURE.
- Over thousands of years, agricultural practices improved
with better tools, methods and knowledge.
- Today, modern agriculture uses advanced tools like
tractors, seed drills, harvesters and modern irrigation
techniques to produce food on a large scale.

Agriculture is essential because it feeds the entire human
population and forms the backbone of the Indian economy.

items.question: Explain the difference between Kharif and Rabi
items.answer:
KHARIF CROPS vs RABI CROPS:

KHARIF CROPS:
- Season: Rainy season (June to September)
- Climate needed: Warm and wet conditions, high rainfall
- Examples: Paddy, Maize, Soyabean, Groundnut, Cotton
- These crops need high water availability for growth

RABI CROPS:
- Season: Winter season (October to March)
- Climate needed: Cool weather during growth, mild sunshine
- Examples: Wheat, Gram, Pea, Mustard, Linseed
- These crops get damaged in heavy rain and need dry harvest

WHY PADDY CANNOT BE GROWN IN WINTER:
Paddy (rice) requires a very large amount of water for its
growth. In India, the rainy season (June-September) provides
the required water through rainfall and filled water bodies.
In winter, rainfall is very low, so sufficient water for
paddy cultivation is not available. Also, paddy requires
warm temperatures for proper germination and growth, which
are not present in winter. Therefore, paddy can only be
grown in the rainy (Kharif) season.

items.question: Write a detailed note on crops - their
items.answer:
CROPS - DEFINITION:
When plants of the same kind are cultivated at one place on
a large scale, they are called a CROP. For example, a wheat
crop means all the plants growing in the field are wheat.

NEED FOR CROPS:
All living organisms require food for energy. Plants make
their own food, but animals including humans cannot. We get
our food from plants, animals or both. To feed a large
population, food must be produced on a large scale through
organised crop cultivation.

TYPES OF CROPS:
Crops are broadly of different types based on what they
produce:
1. CEREAL CROPS: Rice, wheat, maize, millets - provide
carbohydrates and energy
2. PULSE CROPS: Gram, pea, lentil, moong - provide proteins
3. OILSEED CROPS: Groundnut, mustard, sunflower, soyabean -
provide oils and fats
4. VEGETABLE CROPS: Potato, tomato, onion - provide vitamins
and minerals
5. FRUIT CROPS: Mango, banana, apple - provide vitamins,
minerals and sugars

IMPORTANCE IN HUMAN LIFE:
1. Crops provide food (carbohydrates, proteins, fats,

3. They provide fodder for animals.
4. Agriculture is the main source of livelihood for a large
part of India's population.

by absorbing CO2 and releasing oxygen.

India's diversity in climate and soil allows a rich variety
of crops to be grown, making it one of the world's major
agricultural countries.

Basic practices of crop production are the series of
activities or tasks undertaken by farmers for growing crops.
These activities are called AGRICULTURAL PRACTICES.

sections.label: Key Points:
points: Cultivation of crops involves several activities undertaken
by farmers over a period of time.
These activities are similar to gardening activities.
The seven basic agricultural practices are:
(i) Preparation of soil
(ii) Sowing
(iii) Adding manure and fertilisers
(iv) Irrigation
(v) Protecting from weeds
(vi) Harvesting
(vii) Storage
Each practice is essential for a good crop yield.
Modern agricultural practices save labour, time and improve
efficiency.

items.question: List any four basic agricultural practices.
items.answer:
Four basic agricultural practices are:
1. PREPARATION OF SOIL - tilling and loosening of soil before
sowing seeds.
2. SOWING - placing good quality seeds at proper depth and
distance in the soil.
3. IRRIGATION - supplying water to crops at regular intervals.
4. HARVESTING - cutting the mature crop from the field.

items.question: Why are agricultural practices important for
items.answer:
Agricultural practices are important because:
1. They ensure systematic and organised crop cultivation which
gives better yield.
2. Each practice like soil preparation, sowing, manuring,
irrigation and weeding directly affects the quality and
quantity of the crop produced.
Without proper agricultural practices, crops may be weak,
the yield may be poor and the food produced may be of low
quality.

items.question: How are the agricultural activities of a farmer
items.answer:
The agricultural activities carried out by a farmer are
similar to those done by a gardener or even by us when we
grow ornamental plants at home. Both involve:

1. SOIL PREPARATION: A gardener loosens and prepares the
soil in pots or garden beds, just like a farmer prepares
the field by ploughing.

2. SOWING/PLANTING: A gardener plants seeds or saplings in
the soil at proper depth, exactly like a farmer sows
seeds at proper depth and spacing.

3. WATERING/IRRIGATION: A gardener waters the plants
regularly, similar to how a farmer irrigates the field.

4. MANURING: A gardener adds compost or fertiliser to pots,
just like a farmer adds manure and fertilisers to the
field.

5. WEEDING: A gardener removes unwanted plants from the
garden, similar to how a farmer removes weeds from the
crop field.

The main difference is the SCALE - a farmer does these
activities on a much larger scale using advanced tools and
machinery.

items.question: Name and describe any three agricultural tools
items.answer:
Three important agricultural tools used in crop production:

1. PLOUGH:
- Used since ancient times for tilling the soil
- Made of wood, drawn by a pair of bulls or other animals
- Contains a strong triangular iron strip called
PLOUGHSHARE, a long log of wood called PLOUGHSHAFT and
a beam placed on the bulls' necks
- Modern iron ploughs have replaced the traditional wooden
ploughs
- Also used for adding fertilisers, removing weeds and
turning soil

2. HOE:
- A simple tool used for removing weeds and loosening soil
- Has a long rod of wood or iron with a strong, broad,
bent plate of iron fixed at one end (works like a blade)
- Pulled by animals

3. CULTIVATOR:
- A modern tool driven by a tractor
- Used for ploughing the field
- Saves both labour and time compared to traditional plough

items.question: Explain how modern agricultural practices differ
items.answer:
TRADITIONAL AGRICULTURAL PRACTICES:
- Used simple hand tools like sickle, bullock plough,
trowel (khurpi), etc.
- Depended mainly on rain water for irrigation (rain-fed
farming)
- Traditional methods of sowing - funnel-shaped tools drawn
by bullocks
- Seed selection was done by experience and observation
- Manuring was done with cattle dung and compost
- Harvesting was done manually by sickle
- Grain separation done by winnowing - throwing grains in
air

MODERN AGRICULTURAL PRACTICES:
- Uses advanced implements like tractors, cultivators, seed
drills, harvesters, combine machines
- Uses modern irrigation methods - sprinkler and drip systems
that conserve water
- Seeds are scientifically tested and selected for high yield
- Chemical fertilisers (urea, NPK) are used for faster growth
- Chemical weedicides (2,4-D) are used to control weeds
- Combine harvester does both harvesting and threshing

DIFFERENCES:
- Modern practices are more efficient, less labour-intensive
and more time-saving
- Modern practices give better and more consistent crop yield
- Traditional practices are cheaper but less efficient
- Modern practices require knowledge of science and technology

items.question: Why is it necessary to carry out agricultural
items.answer:
Agricultural practices must be carried out in a proper
sequence because each step prepares the conditions for the
next step. If the sequence is not followed, the crop will
fail or yield poorly.

PROPER SEQUENCE using sugarcane as an example:
Step 1: PREPARATION OF SOIL - Plough and level the field to
loosen the soil so roots can penetrate and breathe.
Step 2: MANURING - Add manure to the field to enrich soil
with nutrients before planting.
Step 3: SOWING/PLANTING - Plant sugarcane stems at proper
depth and spacing.
Step 4: IRRIGATION - Provide water at regular intervals for
proper growth.
Step 5: WEEDING - Remove unwanted weeds that compete with
sugarcane for water and nutrients.
Step 6: HARVESTING - Cut the mature sugarcane after 10-12
months.
Step 7: SENDING TO SUGAR FACTORY - Transport harvested
sugarcane for processing.

If soil is not prepared before sowing, roots cannot grow
deep and the plant will be weak. If irrigation is not done,
the plant will wilt and die. If weeds are not removed, they
will take away the nutrients meant for the crop. Therefore,
proper sequence is absolutely essential.

items.question: Write a detailed account of the seven basic
items.answer:
SEVEN BASIC AGRICULTURAL PRACTICES

1. PREPARATION OF SOIL:
The first and most important step. The soil is loosened and
turned using a plough (tilling/ploughing). This:
- Allows roots to penetrate deep into the soil
- Allows roots to breathe easily
- Brings nutrient-rich soil from below to the top
- Helps earthworms and microbes to grow and add humus
- Allows water to penetrate deep
- Helps in mixing manure with soil
Tools: Plough (traditional), Hoe, Cultivator (modern)

2. SOWING:
Placing seeds in the prepared soil at proper depth and spacing.
Before sowing, healthy seeds are selected (damaged seeds
float on water). Proper spacing ensures each plant gets
sufficient sunlight, water and nutrients.
Tools: Traditional funnel tool, Seed drill (modern)

3. ADDING MANURE AND FERTILISERS:
Continuous cultivation removes nutrients from soil. These
are replenished by adding:
- MANURE: Organic substance from decomposed plant/animal
waste. Improves soil texture and water-holding capacity.
- FERTILISERS: Chemical salts like urea, NPK, super
phosphate. Rich in specific nutrients.
Crop rotation also naturally replenishes nitrogen.

4. IRRIGATION:
Supplying water to crops at regular intervals. Water is
needed for germination, nutrient transport and growth.
Sources: Wells, tubewells, ponds, rivers, dams, canals.
Modern methods: Sprinkler system, Drip system (most
efficient - no wastage, water falls near roots).

5. PROTECTION FROM WEEDS:
Weeds are unwanted plants that compete with the crop for
water, nutrients, space and light. They must be removed.
Methods: Tilling before sowing, manual removal with khurpi,
spraying weedicides (e.g., 2,4-D) during vegetative growth.
Best time: Before weeds produce flowers and seeds.

6. HARVESTING:
Cutting the mature crop (takes 3-4 months for cereal crops).
Done manually with a sickle or by combine harvester.
After harvesting: THRESHING - separating grain from chaff.
Small farmers: Winnowing machine; Large scale: Combine.

7. STORAGE:
Protecting harvested grains from moisture, insects, rats
and microorganisms. Grains are first dried in the sun.
Small scale: Jute bags, dried neem leaves added at home.
Large scale: Silos and granaries with chemical treatment
to protect from pests.

Each practice is important - skipping or doing poorly at
any one step can reduce yield or damage the crop. Together,
they ensure food security for the entire population.

items.question: What is tilling? Why is it important?
items.answer:
TILLING (also called PLOUGHING) is the process of loosening
and turning of the soil before sowing seeds.
It is important because:
1. It allows roots to penetrate deep into the soil.
2. It allows roots to breathe easily as loose soil has more
air spaces.
3. It brings nutrient-rich soil from below to the top for
plants to use.
4. It helps earthworms and microbes grow, which further
loosen the soil and add humus.

items.question: Name the three main parts of a plough and their
items.answer:
Three main parts of a plough:
1. PLOUGHSHARE: Strong triangular iron strip - cuts and turns
the soil.
2. PLOUGHSHAFT: Long log of wood - forms the main body of the
plough, connects ploughshare to the beam.
3. BEAM: Placed on the bulls' necks - transmits the pulling
force from the bulls to the ploughshaft and ploughshare.

items.question: Describe three agricultural implements used for
items.answer:
Three agricultural implements used for preparation of soil:

1. PLOUGH:
Used since ancient times. Made of wood with a strong
triangular iron strip (ploughshare) at the bottom. Drawn by
a pair of bulls. Used for tilling, turning soil, adding
fertilisers and removing weeds. Traditional wooden ploughs
are now being replaced by iron ploughs.

2. HOE:
A simple tool with a long rod and a strong broad bent iron
plate at one end (like a blade). Pulled by animals. Used for
removing weeds and loosening the soil.

3. CULTIVATOR:
A modern tractor-driven implement. Performs the same function
as the plough but much faster, saving time and labour. Now
widely used in modern farming.

items.question: Why does loosening of soil allow roots to
items.answer:
Soil contains minerals, water, AIR and living organisms.
When soil is loosened by tilling:
- Air spaces are created in the soil between soil particles.
- These air spaces allow roots to get the oxygen they need
for RESPIRATION (breathing).
- Plant roots need oxygen for energy to absorb water and
minerals from the soil.
- Roots can also penetrate deep into the loose soil to find
water and nutrients.
If the soil is hard and compact (not loosened):
- There are very few air spaces.
- Roots cannot penetrate deep.
- Roots cannot get enough oxygen and they suffocate.
- Plants become weak and their growth is stunted.
Therefore, loosening of soil is essential for healthy root
growth and strong plants.

items.question: Why is preparation of soil considered the most
items.answer:
Preparation of soil is considered the most important step
in crop production for the following reasons:

1. HELPS ROOT GROWTH:
Loose soil allows plant roots to penetrate deep into the
soil. Deep roots can absorb more water and minerals, making
the plant strong and healthy.

2. IMPROVES AERATION:
Loose soil has air spaces that allow roots to breathe. Roots
need oxygen for respiration to generate energy for absorbing
water and nutrients.

3. BRINGS NUTRIENTS TO TOP LAYER:
Only the top few centimetres of soil support plant growth.
Tilling turns the soil and brings nutrient-rich soil from
deeper layers to the top, making it available for plants.

4. PROMOTES MICROBES AND EARTHWORMS:
Loosened soil encourages the growth of earthworms and
microbes. These organisms further loosen the soil and add
humus (decomposed organic matter) which improves soil
fertility.

5. HELPS IN MANURING:
When manure is added before tilling, it gets properly mixed
with the soil during ploughing, ensuring uniform distribution
of nutrients throughout the field.

6. AIDS WATER PENETRATION:
Loose soil allows rainwater and irrigation water to penetrate
deep into the soil, reducing water runoff and ensuring water
reaches the roots.

If soil is not properly prepared, seeds may not germinate
well, roots may not grow deep, and the overall crop yield
will be poor.

items.question: What happens if the soil is dry before
items.answer:
PROBLEM WITH DRY SOIL:
When soil is very dry before ploughing, it becomes very hard
and compacted. Ploughing dry, hard soil creates many
problems:
- The soil breaks into very large clumps called CRUMBS
instead of loose, fine particles.
- Large clumps are difficult to break and are not suitable
for sowing seeds directly.
- The ploughshare has difficulty cutting through very hard,
dry soil.
- The soil does not mix well with manure if added.

MEASURES THE FARMER SHOULD TAKE:
1. WATER THE FIELD FIRST: Before ploughing very dry soil,
the farmer should water it to moisten it. Moist soil is
easier to plough and breaks into smaller, manageable
pieces.

2. BREAK LARGE CLUMPS: After ploughing, if large clumps
(crumbs) are formed, the farmer should use a LEVELLER
to break them into smaller pieces.

3. LEVEL THE FIELD: After breaking clumps, the field should
be levelled using a leveller. Levelling is beneficial for:
- Uniform sowing of seeds
- Uniform distribution of irrigation water
- Preventing waterlogging in low areas

4. ADD MANURE: Manure can be added to dry soil before
watering and ploughing so it gets mixed into the soil
during ploughing.

These measures ensure the soil is properly prepared and
ready for sowing.

items.question: Give a detailed account of the tools used for
items.answer:
TOOLS FOR PREPARATION OF SOIL

The main tools used for preparation of soil are the plough,
hoe and cultivator. Let us study each in detail.

A. PLOUGH (Traditional Tool):
DESCRIPTION:
- Used since ancient times for tilling the soil
- Also used for adding fertilisers, removing weeds, turning
soil
- Made of wood; drawn by a pair of bulls, horses or camels

PARTS:
1. PLOUGHSHARE: Strong triangular iron strip at the bottom -
cuts and turns the soil as the plough moves forward.
2. PLOUGHSHAFT: Long log of wood forming the main body; the
ploughshare is attached to one end.
3. BEAM: Horizontal piece placed on the bulls' necks; a
handle is at the other end of the shaft for the farmer
to guide the plough.

WORKING: Bulls pull the beam which is connected to the
ploughshaft. The ploughshare cuts into the soil, loosening
and turning it. One pair of bulls can easily operate the
plough.

NOTE: The traditional indigenous wooden plough is
increasingly being replaced by iron ploughs which are
stronger and more durable.

B. HOE (Simple Traditional Tool):
DESCRIPTION:
- Simple tool for removing weeds and loosening soil
- Has a long rod of wood or iron
- A strong, broad, bent iron plate is fixed at one end
(works like a blade)
- Pulled by animals

C. CULTIVATOR (Modern Tool):
DESCRIPTION:
- A modern agricultural implement
- Driven by a tractor (not animals)
- Multiple blades that loosen and aerate the soil
- Saves labour and time significantly

COMPARISON: TRADITIONAL vs MODERN:

PLOUGH (Traditional):
- Drawn by animals (bulls)
- Slower process
- Less expensive to operate
- More labour required
- Still widely used in small farms and rural areas

CULTIVATOR (Modern):
- Driven by tractor
- Much faster - covers more land in less time
- Requires fuel (diesel) - higher operating cost
- Less labour required
- Used in large farms and modern agriculture

After ploughing (by either method), large clumps of soil
(crumbs) may form. These are broken by a LEVELLER. Levelling
the ploughed field is also important for:
- Uniform sowing
- Proper irrigation (water does not collect in low areas)

The choice of tool depends on the size of the farm, the
farmer's resources, and local conditions.

sections.label: Definition:
sections.text:
Sowing is the process of putting seeds into the soil at
proper depth and with proper spacing. It is one of the most
important agricultural practices as the quality of seeds and
the method of sowing directly affects the crop yield.

sections.label: Key Points:
points: Before sowing, good quality, clean and healthy seeds of a
good variety must be selected.
SEED SELECTION: Damaged seeds float on water (they are
hollow and lighter); healthy seeds sink (heavier). Farmers
prefer seeds that give high yield.
Seeds of paddy are first grown in a nursery and seedlings
are then transplanted to the main field.
Appropriate distance between seeds is necessary to avoid
overcrowding - plants need sufficient sunlight, nutrients
and water.
At times a few plants may be removed to prevent
overcrowding.
Sowing is done by:
(a) TRADITIONAL TOOL: Funnel-shaped tool
(b) SEED DRILL: Modern machine driven by tractor
TRADITIONAL TOOL:
Funnel-shaped tool
Seeds filled into the funnel
Pass down through 2-3 pipes with sharp ends
Sharp ends pierce the soil and place seeds at proper depth
Drawn by animals
SEED DRILL (Modern):
Used with the help of tractors
Sows seeds uniformly at equal distance and equal depth
Ensures seeds get covered by soil after sowing
Protects seeds from being eaten by birds
Saves time and labour

items.question: What is sowing? How are damaged seeds identified?
items.answer:
SOWING is the process of putting seeds into the prepared soil
at proper depth and with proper spacing.

IDENTIFYING DAMAGED SEEDS:
Damaged seeds can be identified by putting them in water.
Damaged seeds have become hollow due to damage, so they are
lighter than good seeds. Lighter damaged seeds FLOAT on water.
Healthy, undamaged seeds are heavier and SINK to the bottom.
This simple water test helps farmers select only healthy seeds
for sowing.

items.question: What are the advantages of using a seed drill
items.answer:
Advantages of seed drill over traditional sowing:
1. UNIFORM SOWING: Seed drill sows seeds at equal distance
and equal depth throughout the field, ensuring uniform
growth of plants.
2. PROTECTS SEEDS: Seeds get covered by soil after sowing,
protecting them from being eaten by birds.
3. SAVES TIME AND LABOUR: A seed drill with a tractor covers
a large area quickly, saving both time and labour.
4. PROPER DEPTH: Ensures all seeds are placed at the correct
depth for germination.

items.question: Why is proper spacing between seeds important?
items.answer:
IMPORTANCE OF PROPER SPACING:
When seeds are sown at appropriate distances from each other:
- Each plant gets sufficient SUNLIGHT for photosynthesis.
- Each plant gets adequate NUTRIENTS from the soil without
competition.
- Each plant gets enough WATER from the soil.
- Air circulation around each plant is good.
- This allows each plant to grow well and produce a good
yield.

WHAT HAPPENS IF SEEDS ARE SOWN TOO CLOSE (OVERCROWDING):
- Plants compete with each other for sunlight, nutrients and
water.
- No plant gets adequate resources as they all share the
limited supply.
- Plants become weak, thin and fail to produce good yield.
- At times, a few plants may have to be removed to prevent
overcrowding after germination.
- The overall crop yield reduces significantly.

Therefore, proper spacing (determined for each type of crop)
is essential for a healthy and productive crop.

items.question: Explain the process of transplanting. Why are
items.answer:
TRANSPLANTING:
Transplanting is the process of growing plants first in a
NURSERY (where they are kept in small pots or beds with
proper care) and then moving the SEEDLINGS (young plants)
to the main field when they are strong enough.

PROCESS:
1. Seeds are sown in a nursery (small, protected area).
2. They are watered and cared for carefully.
3. When seedlings are of appropriate size, they are
TRANSPLANTED manually to the main field.

WHY PADDY IS FIRST GROWN IN A NURSERY:
1. DELICATE EARLY STAGE: Paddy seeds are delicate during
germination and early growth. A nursery provides
controlled conditions for the seeds to sprout safely.
2. WATER MANAGEMENT: Paddy fields need to be flooded with
water. Seeds cannot be sown directly in flooded fields.
Seedlings grown in nursery are strong enough to be
transplanted into flooded fields.
3. BETTER SURVIVAL RATE: Seedlings from nursery are already
established and strong, so they survive better when
transplanted to field conditions.
4. WEED CONTROL: While seedlings grow in nursery, the main
field can be prepared and cleared of weeds before
transplanting.

items.question: Compare the traditional method of sowing with
items.answer:
COMPARISON OF TRADITIONAL vs SEED DRILL METHOD

TRADITIONAL METHOD (Funnel-shaped tool):
DESCRIPTION: A funnel-shaped tool with 2-3 pipes having sharp
ends. Seeds are filled in the funnel and pass through the
pipes. The sharp ends pierce the soil and place seeds.
Drawn by animals (bullocks).

ADVANTAGES:
- Simple to operate
- Does not require fuel or electricity
- Cheap

DISADVANTAGES:
- Seeds may not be placed at equal distances
- Depth of sowing may not be uniform
- Slow process - covers less area
- Requires both human skill and animal power

SEED DRILL METHOD (Modern):
DESCRIPTION: A tractor-driven machine with multiple seed
compartments and tubes. Sows seeds at equal spacing and
equal depth. Seeds are covered by soil automatically.

ADVANTAGES:
- Uniform sowing - equal distance and depth throughout field
- Seeds are covered by soil automatically - protected from
birds
- Much faster - saves time
- Less labour required
- Gives better and more uniform crop growth

DISADVANTAGES:
- Requires tractor and fuel - higher cost
- Requires technical knowledge to operate
- Not suitable for small farms

CONCLUSION:
The seed drill is BETTER for large-scale farming because it
ensures uniform seed placement, saves time and labour, and
leads to more consistent and better crop yield. However, for
small farms with limited resources, the traditional method
may still be practical.

items.question: What is the importance of seed selection before
items.answer:
IMPORTANCE OF SEED SELECTION:
The quality of seeds directly determines the quality and
quantity of the crop. If poor quality seeds are sown:
- Germination rate will be low (some seeds won't sprout)
- Plants that grow from poor seeds will be weak
- Yield will be poor - both in quantity and quality
- Farmer's efforts in soil preparation, irrigation and
manuring will be wasted

Therefore, before sowing, farmers select:
- GOOD QUALITY seeds from a trusted source
- CLEAN seeds (free from dirt and foreign matter)
- HEALTHY seeds (not damaged, shrivelled or infected)
- HIGH-YIELDING VARIETY seeds that give more produce

WATER TEST FOR SEED SELECTION:
PROCEDURE:
1. Take a vessel or beaker and fill it with water.
2. Put a handful of seeds (e.g., wheat or gram) and stir.
3. Wait for some time and observe.

OBSERVATION AND REASON:
- HEALTHY SEEDS SINK: Good seeds are fully developed with
endosperm (food) inside. They are heavier and sink to
the bottom.
- DAMAGED SEEDS FLOAT: Damaged seeds have become hollow
(the food inside is used up or damaged). They are lighter
than water, so they float.

CONCLUSION:
Seeds that float are discarded; seeds that sink are
collected and used for sowing. This simple test takes only
a few minutes and significantly improves the quality of
sowing.

items.question: Write a comprehensive note on sowing -

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
Sowing is the process of placing seeds in the prepared soil
at proper depth and with proper spacing.

IMPORTANCE OF SOWING:
Sowing is a critical step because:
1. The quality of seeds determines the quality of the crop.
2. Proper spacing ensures each plant gets adequate sunlight,
water and nutrients.
3. Proper depth ensures good germination and strong root
development.
4. Poor sowing leads to poor yield regardless of how well
other practices are carried out.

SEED SELECTION:
Before sowing, seeds must be carefully selected.
CHARACTERISTICS OF GOOD SEEDS:
- They should be from a good variety known for high yield
- They should be healthy, fully developed and undamaged
- They should be clean and free from disease
- They should be of uniform size

WATER TEST:
Put seeds in water. Good healthy seeds sink (heavier);
damaged hollow seeds float (lighter). Only sinking seeds
should be used.

APPROPRIATE SPACING:
Each crop requires a specific distance between seeds for
proper growth. Seeds sown at proper distance:
- Allow roots to spread without competition
- Allow leaves to get adequate sunlight
- Allow air to circulate and prevent fungal diseases
- Each plant gets full share of soil nutrients and water

METHODS OF SOWING:
1. TRADITIONAL METHOD (Funnel-shaped tool):
- Seeds placed in funnel
- Pass down through 2-3 pipes with sharp ends
- Sharp ends pierce soil and deposit seeds
- Drawn by animals
- Simple but may lack uniformity

2. SEED DRILL (Modern method):
- Tractor-driven machine
- Sows seeds at equal distance and depth
- Seeds covered by soil automatically
- Fast, uniform and labour-saving
- Prevents birds from eating seeds

3. TRANSPLANTING:
- Used for paddy, some vegetables and flowering plants
- Seeds first grown in nursery
- Seedlings transplanted to main field when strong
- Some forest plants and flowering plants also grown
in nursery and transplanted

PRECAUTIONS DURING SOWING:
- Always test seeds in water before sowing
- Follow recommended depth for each crop
- Maintain recommended spacing between seeds
- Sow at the right time of season for the crop
- Ensure soil is properly prepared before sowing
- If any seeds are sown in nursery first, transplant
seedlings at the right stage - not too early or too late

A good sowing practice sets the foundation for the entire
crop cycle. The farmer's effort in subsequent steps like
irrigation and manuring will only succeed if sowing is done
correctly.

sections.label: Definition:
sections.text:
Manure and fertilisers are the substances added to the soil
in the form of nutrients for the healthy growth of plants.
Replenishing the soil with nutrients is essential for
maintaining soil fertility.

sections.label: Key Points:
points: Soil supplies mineral nutrients to crop plants.
Continuous cultivation makes the soil poor in nutrients.
Farmers must add manure/fertilisers to replenish nutrients
this is called MANURING.
Improper or insufficient manuring results in weak plants.
MANURE:
Organic substance obtained from decomposition of plant or
animal wastes.
Farmers dump plant and animal waste in pits at open places
and allow it to DECOMPOSE.
Decomposition is caused by MICROORGANISMS.
The decomposed matter is used as organic manure.
ADVANTAGES OF MANURE over Fertilisers:
Enhances the WATER HOLDING CAPACITY of soil.
Makes soil POROUS - exchange of gases becomes easy.
Increases number of FRIENDLY MICROBES in soil.
Improves the TEXTURE of soil.
Adds HUMUS to the soil.
FERTILISERS:
Chemicals which are RICH IN PARTICULAR NUTRIENTS.
Produced in FACTORIES (not from natural decomposition).
Examples: Urea, Ammonium sulphate, Super phosphate,
Potash, NPK (Nitrogen, Phosphorus, Potassium).
Help farmers get better yield of crops like wheat, paddy
and maize.
PROBLEMS with excessive use:
Makes soil LESS FERTILE over time.
Becomes source of WATER POLLUTION.
MANURE vs FERTILISER: Table 1.1
FERTILISER:
1. Man-made inorganic salt
2. Prepared in factories
3. Does not provide any humus to soil
4. Very rich in plant nutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus,
potassium)
MANURE:
1. Natural substance from decomposition of cattle dung and
plant residues
2. Can be prepared in the fields
3. Provides a lot of humus to soil
4. Relatively less rich in plant nutrients
CROP ROTATION:
Growing different crops alternately in the same field.
Earlier, farmers in northern India grew legumes as fodder
in one season and wheat in the next.
Legume roots have RHIZOBIUM bacteria in nodules that FIX
ATMOSPHERIC NITROGEN, replenishing soil with nitrogen.
Farmers are encouraged to adopt crop rotation.

items.question: What are fertilisers? Give two examples.
items.answer:
FERTILISERS are chemicals which are rich in particular
nutrients like nitrogen, phosphorus or potassium. They are
prepared in factories (not from natural decomposition).
Examples:
1. Urea - rich in nitrogen
2. NPK (Nitrogen, Phosphorus, Potassium) - provides three
major nutrients

items.question: What is manure? How is it prepared?
items.answer:
MANURE is an organic substance obtained from the
decomposition of plant or animal wastes.
PREPARATION:
Farmers dump plant and animal waste (like cattle dung, crop
residues, vegetable peels) in pits at open places. These
are allowed to decompose. The decomposition is caused by
microorganisms. After decomposition, the decomposed matter
is used as organic manure.

items.question: Why is manure considered better than fertilisers
items.answer:
Manure is considered better than fertilisers for maintaining
long-term soil fertility because:

1. IMPROVES SOIL TEXTURE: Manure adds humus (decomposed
organic matter) which improves the texture of soil,
making it soft and crumbly.

2. ENHANCES WATER HOLDING CAPACITY: Humus in manure makes
the soil hold more water, reducing the need for frequent
irrigation.

3. MAKES SOIL POROUS: Manure makes the soil porous, allowing
easy exchange of gases (oxygen and carbon dioxide) so
roots can breathe.

4. INCREASES FRIENDLY MICROBES: Manure increases the number
of beneficial microorganisms in the soil that help
decompose organic matter and release nutrients.

5. NO POLLUTION: Unlike fertilisers, excessive use of manure
does not cause water pollution or reduce soil fertility.

In contrast, excessive use of chemical fertilisers makes the
soil less fertile over time and causes water pollution.
Therefore, organic manure is better for sustainable
agriculture.

items.question: What is crop rotation? How does it help in
items.answer:
CROP ROTATION is the practice of growing different types of
crops alternately in the same field over different seasons.

HOW IT HELPS IN MAINTAINING SOIL FERTILITY:
When the same crop is grown in a field season after season,
the same nutrients are depleted from the soil each time.
Crop rotation helps in the following ways:

1. NITROGEN REPLENISHMENT: When LEGUMINOUS CROPS (like gram,
pea, moong, lentil) are grown in one season, their roots
have RHIZOBIUM bacteria in root nodules. These bacteria
FIX ATMOSPHERIC NITROGEN and convert it into nitrogen
compounds in the soil, naturally replenishing the soil's
nitrogen content.

2. DIFFERENT NUTRIENTS DEPLETED: Different crops use
different nutrients from the soil. By rotating crops,
no single nutrient gets completely exhausted.

3. PRACTICAL EXAMPLE: Earlier, farmers in northern India
grew legumes as fodder in one season and wheat in the
next. The legumes fixed nitrogen, which benefited the
wheat crop in the following season.

This natural and economical method reduces the need for
chemical fertilisers and maintains soil health in the
long run.

items.question: Explain the differences between manure and
items.answer:
DIFFERENCES BETWEEN MANURE AND FERTILISERS:

MANURE:
- ORIGIN: Natural; obtained from decomposition of plant and
animal wastes by microorganisms.
- NUTRIENT CONTENT: Relatively less rich in specific
nutrients.
- HUMUS: Provides a lot of humus to soil.
- SOIL TEXTURE: Improves soil texture, water holding capacity
and porosity.
- PREPARATION: Can be prepared in the fields by farmers.
- EFFECT ON SOIL: Long-term improvement of soil health.
- POLLUTION: Does not cause water pollution.

FERTILISERS:
- ORIGIN: Man-made inorganic salts prepared in factories.
- NUTRIENT CONTENT: Very rich in specific plant nutrients
(nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium).
- HUMUS: Does not provide any humus to soil.
- SOIL TEXTURE: Does not improve soil texture.
- PREPARATION: Prepared in factories; expensive.
- EFFECT ON SOIL: Long-term use reduces soil fertility.
- POLLUTION: Excessive use causes water pollution.

WHY USE OF CHEMICAL FERTILISERS SHOULD BE CONTROLLED:

1. REDUCES SOIL FERTILITY: Excessive use of chemical
fertilisers over the years destroys the soil's natural
structure and reduces its fertility.

2. WATER POLLUTION: Fertilisers dissolve in irrigation water
and run off into rivers, ponds and lakes, causing water
pollution (eutrophication).

3. DESTROYS MICROBES: Chemical fertilisers can kill beneficial
soil microorganisms, further damaging soil health.

4. SUSTAINABLE AGRICULTURE: To maintain long-term
agricultural productivity, it is better to use organic
manure or leave the field fallow (uncultivated) between
two crops rather than over-relying on chemical
fertilisers.

items.question: What happens to soil nutrients when crops are
items.answer:
EFFECT OF CONTINUOUS CULTIVATION ON SOIL NUTRIENTS:

Soil supplies mineral nutrients to crop plants. These
nutrients include nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and
others which are essential for plant growth. When crops are
grown continuously in the same field:

1. NUTRIENTS GET DEPLETED: Plants absorb nutrients from the
soil for their growth. After each crop is harvested, those
nutrients are removed from the field along with the crop.
2. SOIL BECOMES POOR: Continuous cultivation without
replenishment makes the soil poor in nutrients.
3. WEAK PLANTS: Plants grown in nutrient-poor soil become
weak and fail to produce good yield.

WAYS TO REPLENISH SOIL NUTRIENTS:

1. ADDING MANURE (MANURING):
Farmers add organic manure made from decomposed plant and
animal waste. This is the most natural method. Manure
replenishes nutrients and also improves soil texture.

2. ADDING FERTILISERS:
Chemical fertilisers like urea, NPK, ammonium sulphate
are added to quickly replenish specific nutrients. Though
effective, they should not be overused.

3. CROP ROTATION:
Growing different crops alternately. Leguminous crops
(gram, pea) grown in one season fix atmospheric nitrogen
and replenish soil nitrogen naturally for the next crop.

4. LEAVING FIELD FALLOW:
Sometimes the field is left uncultivated (fallow) between
two crops. This allows the soil to naturally regenerate
its nutrients.

5. VERMICOMPOSTING:
Using earthworms to convert organic waste into nutrient-
rich compost (vermicompost) which is added to the soil.

items.question: Write a detailed note on the role of manure and
items.answer:
MANURE AND FERTILISERS IN CROP PRODUCTION

INTRODUCTION:
Plants need nutrients for their growth. The main nutrients
required are nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and potassium (K),
along with many other minerals. Soil supplies these nutrients
to crops. Continuous cultivation depletes the soil of these
nutrients. To maintain soil fertility and ensure good crop
yield, farmers add MANURE and FERTILISERS to the soil.

A. MANURE - ORGANIC NUTRIENT SUPPLEMENT

DEFINITION: Organic substance obtained from decomposition of
plant and animal waste.

PREPARATION:
Farmers collect plant waste, animal dung, crop residues and
other organic waste. These are collected in pits at open
places and left to decompose. Microorganisms (bacteria,
fungi) break down the complex organic matter into simpler
substances over weeks to months. The resulting dark, crumbly
material is organic manure.

TYPES:
1. FARMYARD MANURE (FYM): From cattle dung, urine, crop
residues mixed together.
2. GREEN MANURE: From green plants (like sunhemp) grown and
ploughed back into the field.
3. VERMICOMPOST: Made using earthworms.
4. COMPOST: From decomposed kitchen and garden waste.

ADVANTAGES OF MANURE:
1. Provides humus - improves soil structure and texture
2. Enhances water holding capacity of soil
3. Makes soil porous - improves aeration
4. Increases population of beneficial microbes
5. Environmentally friendly - no pollution
6. Can be made by farmers themselves - economical
7. Sustainable - long-term improvement of soil health

DISADVANTAGES:
1. Less rich in specific nutrients
2. Takes time to prepare
3. Bulky - difficult to transport in large quantities
4. Nutrients may not be immediately available to plants

B. FERTILISERS - CHEMICAL NUTRIENT SUPPLEMENT

DEFINITION: Man-made inorganic chemicals rich in specific
plant nutrients.

EXAMPLES:
1. NITROGEN FERTILISERS: Urea, Ammonium sulphate - promote
leafy vegetative growth
2. PHOSPHORUS FERTILISERS: Super phosphate - promote root
and flower development
3. POTASSIUM FERTILISERS: Potash - promote disease resistance
4. MIXED FERTILISERS: NPK - provide all three major nutrients

ADVANTAGES:
1. Very rich in specific nutrients - quick results
2. Easy to store, transport and apply
3. Small amounts needed for good effect
4. Immediately available to plants

DISADVANTAGES:
1. Excessive use reduces soil fertility over time
2. Causes water pollution by running into water bodies
3. May kill beneficial soil microorganisms
4. Does not add humus to soil
5. Expensive - not affordable for all farmers

C. CROP ROTATION - NATURAL NUTRIENT REPLENISHMENT

Growing leguminous crops (pea, gram, lentil) in one season
fixes atmospheric nitrogen through Rhizobium bacteria in
root nodules. This naturally enriches the soil with nitrogen
for the next crop.

BEST PRACTICES (What farmers should do):
1. Use organic manure as the primary nutrient source.
2. Use chemical fertilisers only when necessary and in
recommended doses.
3. Practice crop rotation to naturally replenish nitrogen.
4. Leave the field fallow between crops occasionally.
5. Do soil testing periodically to know which nutrients are
deficient.
6. Avoid excessive use of chemical fertilisers to prevent
soil degradation and water pollution.

By combining manure, limited fertiliser use and crop
rotation, farmers can maintain long-term soil fertility and
ensure sustainable crop production.

sections.text:
The supply of water to crops at regular intervals is called
IRRIGATION. Water is essential for the germination of seeds,
the transport of nutrients and the overall growth and
development of plants.

sections.label: Key Points:
points: All living beings need water to live.
Water is absorbed by plant roots; nutrients and fertilisers
dissolved in water are transported to all parts of plant.
Plants contain nearly 90% water.
Germination of seeds does not take place under dry
conditions.
Water also PROTECTS crops from frost and hot air currents.
The time and frequency of irrigation varies from crop to
crop, soil to soil and season to season.
In summer, frequency of watering is higher due to increased
rate of evaporation.
SOURCES OF IRRIGATION:
Wells, tubewells, ponds, lakes, rivers, dams, canals.
TRADITIONAL METHODS OF IRRIGATION:
Water is lifted from wells, lakes, canals by different
methods. Cattle or human labour is used - cheaper but less
efficient.
1. MOAT (pulley-system)
2. CHAIN PUMP
3. DHEKLI
4. RAHAT (lever system)
MODERN METHODS OF IRRIGATION:
Help use water economically.
(i) SPRINKLER SYSTEM:
Useful on uneven land where sufficient water is not
available.
Perpendicular pipes with ROTATING NOZZLES on top joined
to main pipeline at regular intervals.
Water flows through main pipe under pressure of a pump.
Escapes from rotating nozzles and gets sprinkled on the
crop as if it is raining.
Useful for lawns, coffee plantations and several other
crops.
DIAGRAM DESCRIPTION: Sprinkler System (Fig. 1.5a)
Diagram shows: A field with pipes and rotating nozzle heads
Parts labeled:
Main pipeline: Supplies water to all branches
Perpendicular pipes: Rise from main pipeline at intervals
Rotating nozzles: At top of perpendicular pipes; sprinkle
water over crops like rain
Working: Water pumped through main pipe, rises through
perpendicular pipes and sprays from rotating nozzles to
simulate rainfall.
(ii) DRIP SYSTEM:
Water falls DROP BY DROP directly near the roots of plants.
Also called DRIP IRRIGATION.
BEST TECHNIQUE for watering fruit plants, gardens, trees.
WATER IS NOT WASTED AT ALL.
A BOON in regions where availability of water is poor.
DIAGRAM DESCRIPTION: Drip System (Fig. 1.5b)
Diagram shows: A field with main pipe and small drip pipes
leading to base of plants
Parts labeled:
Main pipe: Supplies water from source
Lateral pipes: Branch from main pipe along plant rows
Drippers/nozzles: At base of each plant, release water
drop by drop
Working: Water flows slowly through lateral pipes and drips
near the root zone of each plant. Very little evaporation
or runoff - maximum water reaches roots directly.

items.question: Name two modern methods of irrigation and state
items.answer:

1. SPRINKLER SYSTEM:
Advantage: Useful on uneven land; simulates rainfall and

items.question: Why is water essential for crop plants? Explain
items.answer:
Water is essential for crop plants for the following reasons:

1. GERMINATION OF SEEDS:
Germination (sprouting of seeds) does not take place under
dry conditions. Water is required to soften the seed coat
and activate the enzymes inside the seed to start the
germination process.

2. TRANSPORT OF NUTRIENTS:
Nutrients dissolved in water are absorbed by the roots and
transported to all parts of the plant through vessels.
Minerals and fertilisers added to the soil reach the
plants only when dissolved in water.

3. PROTECTION FROM EXTREME WEATHER:
Water in the soil and on the plants' surface protects the
crop from frost (extreme cold) and hot air currents. It
also maintains the moisture of the soil for healthy crop
growth.

Additionally, plants contain nearly 90% water and need
continuous water supply for photosynthesis and other
metabolic activities.

items.question: Describe the sprinkler system of irrigation.
items.answer:
SPRINKLER SYSTEM:
DESCRIPTION:
- Perpendicular pipes are joined to a main pipeline at
regular intervals.
- Each perpendicular pipe has a ROTATING NOZZLE at the top.
- Water is pumped through the main pipeline under pressure.
- When water reaches the perpendicular pipes, it rises up
and escapes through the rotating nozzles.
- The rotating nozzles sprinkle water over the crop like
rain, distributing it uniformly over a large area.

WHERE IT IS MOST USEFUL:
1. UNEVEN LAND: Sprinkler is very useful on uneven land
where it is difficult to direct water by gravity.
2. WHEN WATER IS SCARCE: It is useful in areas where
sufficient water is not always available, as it
distributes water more efficiently than flooding the
field.
3. SPECIFIC CROPS: Very useful for lawns, coffee
plantations, tea gardens and several other crops that
benefit from overhead watering.

items.question: Compare traditional and modern methods of
items.answer:
TRADITIONAL METHODS OF IRRIGATION:

1. MOAT (Pulley-system):
Water lifted from wells using a pulley, rope and bucket.
Animals or humans do the lifting.

2. CHAIN PUMP:
A chain with buckets attached is lowered into water.
Animals rotate the chain; buckets scoop water and
discharge it into the irrigation channel.

3. DHEKLI:
A pole balanced on a pivot with a bucket on one end and
counterweight on the other. Tilted down to fill bucket,
then raised to pour water.

4. RAHAT (Lever system):
Driven by cattle; uses a chain of containers to lift
water from well.

CHARACTERISTICS OF TRADITIONAL METHODS:
- Use CATTLE or human labour
- CHEAPER to operate (no fuel cost)
- LESS EFFICIENT - slow and covers less area
- Suitable for small farms and where water is available
in wells

MODERN METHODS OF IRRIGATION:

1. SPRINKLER SYSTEM:
Uses pipes and rotating nozzles to sprinkle water over
crops. Simulates rainfall. Uses pump.

2. DRIP SYSTEM:
Water drips slowly near the roots of plants through a
network of pipes and drippers.

CHARACTERISTICS OF MODERN METHODS:
- Use PUMPS and pipelines (need fuel/electricity)
- Higher cost of installation and operation
- MUCH MORE EFFICIENT - water used economically
- Cover large areas quickly
- Can be automated

COMPARISON:
Modern methods are MORE EFFICIENT because:
1. Water is used economically - less wastage through
evaporation and runoff.
2. Drip system is the most efficient - water falls directly
near roots, zero wastage.
3. Cover large areas quickly.
4. Suitable for all land types including uneven land.
5. Can work in areas with limited water supply.

Traditional methods are cheaper but cannot meet the
irrigation needs of large modern farms and areas with
water scarcity.

items.question: Explain the drip system of irrigation. Why is
items.answer:
DRIP SYSTEM OF IRRIGATION:

DESCRIPTION:
In the drip system, water is supplied to the field through
a network of pipes. Small holes or drippers are placed at
the base of each plant. Water flows very slowly through
these pipes and DRIPS directly near the ROOTS of each plant.

HOW IT WORKS:
1. A main pipe carries water from the source (tank or pump).
2. Smaller lateral pipes branch off from the main pipe and
run along rows of plants.
3. Each lateral pipe has small drippers placed at regular
intervals near each plant's base.
4. Water flows through the dripper and falls drop by drop
directly near the root zone.

WHY IT IS CALLED THE BEST TECHNIQUE:
1. ZERO WATER WASTAGE: Water falls directly near the roots
where the plant can immediately absorb it. There is no
water flowing between plants where it would be wasted.
2. NO EVAPORATION: Since water goes directly to roots and
does not wet the leaves or soil surface, very little
water is lost to evaporation.
3. NO RUNOFF: Water does not run off from the field as in
flood irrigation.
4. PREVENTS WEED GROWTH: Since only the area near each plant
is watered, weeds in between plants do not get water and
grow less.
5. SUITABLE FOR ALL PLANTS: Works for trees, fruit plants,
gardens and vegetable crops.

WHEN IT IS MOST BENEFICIAL:
1. WATER-SCARCE REGIONS: A great boon in regions where
water availability is poor - every drop of water is
used effectively.
2. FRUIT PLANTS AND TREES: Best for orchards and fruit
gardens where water needs to reach deep root systems.
3. GARDEN AND VEGETABLE CROPS: Used in kitchen gardens and
commercial vegetable farms.
4. SANDY SOILS: In sandy soils that do not hold water well,
drip irrigation ensures water reaches roots before
draining away.

items.question: Write a detailed account of the importance of

sections.label: DEFINITION AND IMPORTANCE:
sections.text:
Irrigation is the controlled supply of water to crops at
regular intervals. It is one of the most critical
agricultural practices because:

1. ESSENTIAL FOR GERMINATION: Seeds do not germinate in dry
soil. Water softens the seed coat and activates
enzymes to start sprouting.

2. NUTRIENT TRANSPORT: All nutrients (from soil, manure,
fertilisers) are dissolved in water and transported to
every cell of the plant through roots and vessels.

3. PHOTOSYNTHESIS: Plants need water for photosynthesis -
the process by which they make their own food using
sunlight, water and CO2.

4. PLANT COMPOSITION: Plants contain nearly 90% water.
Without adequate water supply, plants wilt and die.

5. PROTECTION: Water protects crops from both frost and
hot air currents.

6. GERMINATION-TO-HARVEST: Water is needed at every stage
of crop growth from germination to flowering and fruit/
grain development.

SOURCES OF IRRIGATION:
1. Wells - traditional, widely used in villages
2. Tubewells - deeper wells with electric pumps
3. Ponds and lakes - natural water bodies
4. Rivers - through canal networks
5. Dams - major irrigation projects; store river water
6. Canals - carry water from rivers and dams to fields

TRADITIONAL METHODS:
Water in wells, lakes and canals is lifted using human or
animal labour. These methods are CHEAPER but LESS EFFICIENT.

1. MOAT (Pulley system): Pulley + rope + bucket; animal
or human power used to lift water from well.
2. CHAIN PUMP: Chain with buckets rotated by animals;
scoops water from source.
3. DHEKLI: Pole balanced on pivot with bucket; manually
tilted to fill and raise water.
4. RAHAT (Lever system): Cattle-driven; chain of containers
lifts water from well.

MODERN METHODS:
Use pumps and pipe networks; help use water ECONOMICALLY.

1. SPRINKLER SYSTEM:
- Pipes with rotating nozzles connected to main pipe
- Water pumped under pressure; sprinkled like rainfall
- Best for uneven land, lawns, coffee plantations

2. DRIP SYSTEM (Most efficient):
- Network of pipes with drippers at base of each plant
- Water falls drop by drop near the root zone
- Zero wastage - no runoff, no evaporation between plants
- Best for fruit trees, gardens, water-scarce regions
- Can be used in all types of land and soil

FREQUENCY OF IRRIGATION:
- Varies from crop to crop (paddy needs more water than
wheat)
- Varies from season to season (more frequent in summer due
to more evaporation)
- Varies from soil to soil (sandy soil needs more frequent
irrigation; clay soil retains water longer)

WATER CONSERVATION:
With growing population and shrinking water resources, it
is essential to use water wisely. Modern methods like
sprinkler and drip irrigation help conserve water. Drip
irrigation is particularly important in water-scarce
regions and is called a "boon" for such areas.

sections.label: Definition:
sections.text:
Weeds are undesirable plants that grow naturally in a crop
field along with the cultivated crop. The process of removing
weeds is called WEEDING. Weeds must be controlled to protect
the crop from competition.

sections.label: Key Points:
points: Weeds compete with crop plants for WATER, NUTRIENTS, SPACE
and LIGHT.
They affect the growth of the crop.
Some weeds interfere even in harvesting.
Some weeds may be poisonous for animals and human beings.
Best time for removal: BEFORE weeds produce flowers and
seeds (before they spread further).
Methods of weeding:
1. Tilling before sowing - uproots and kills weeds, weeds

2. Manual removal - physically uprooting or cutting weeds
close to ground, using KHURPI (from time to time).
A seed drill can also be used to uproot weeds.
3. Chemical method - using WEEDICIDES (e.g., 2,4-D)
sprayed in the fields. Kills weeds but does not damage
the crop.
WEEDICIDES:
Chemical sprays like 2,4-D.
Sprayed during vegetative growth of weeds (before

Spraying weedicides may AFFECT HEALTH of farmers who

Precautions: Farmers should cover nose and mouth with

items.question: What are weeds? Give two examples of problems
items.answer:
WEEDS are undesirable plants that grow naturally in crop
fields along with the cultivated crop without being
intentionally planted.
Two problems caused by weeds:
1. Weeds COMPETE with crop plants for water, nutrients,
space and light, reducing the crop's share of resources
and making it weak.
2. Some weeds are POISONOUS for animals and human beings,
making them dangerous especially if they get mixed with

items.question: What are weedicides? Give one precaution while
items.answer:
WEEDICIDES are chemicals (like 2,4-D) that are sprayed in
fields to kill weeds without damaging the crop plants.
They are diluted with water to the required concentration and
sprayed using a sprayer.

PRECAUTION:
Spraying weedicides may affect the health of the person

items.question: Describe three methods of removing weeds from
items.answer:
Three methods of removing weeds from crop fields:

1. TILLING BEFORE SOWING:
When the field is ploughed and tilled before sowing,
weeds already growing in the field are uprooted and
killed. The uprooted weeds dry up in the sun and get
mixed with the soil during further tilling, adding
organic matter to the soil. This is the most basic
method of weed control.

2. MANUAL REMOVAL (Physical method):
Weeds are physically uprooted or cut close to the ground
using a hand tool called KHURPI. This is done from time
to time as weeds grow. A seed drill can also be used to
uproot weeds. Manual removal is best done before weeds
produce flowers and seeds, to prevent further spread.

3. CHEMICAL METHOD (Weedicides):
Chemicals called WEEDICIDES (e.g., 2,4-D) are diluted
with water and sprayed in the field using a sprayer.
They kill the weeds without damaging the main crop. They
are most effective when sprayed during the vegetative
growth of weeds, before they flower and produce seeds.
Farmers must take precautions while spraying - covering
nose and mouth with cloth.

items.question: Why is it important to remove weeds before they
items.answer:
It is very important to remove weeds BEFORE they produce
flowers and seeds for the following reasons:

1. PREVENTS SEED DISPERSAL: Once weeds produce seeds, the
seeds get dispersed by wind, water, animals or birds to
different parts of the field. This means new weed plants
will grow in many more places, making the weed problem
much worse.

2. PREVENTS SPREAD: If weeds are allowed to flower and form
seeds, the number of weed plants in the field multiplies
rapidly over subsequent seasons. Controlling weeds
becomes much more difficult once they have seeded.

3. SAVES THE CROP: Weeds compete with the crop for water,
nutrients, space and light. The longer weeds grow, the
more resources they consume at the expense of the crop.
Early removal saves the crop from prolonged competition.

4. MOST EFFECTIVE TIMING: Weedicides are also most effective
when sprayed during the vegetative growth stage (before
flowering). Spraying after seed formation is less
effective as the seeds have already been produced.

The best time for removal of weeds is thus before they
produce flowers and seeds - ideally during the early stages
of weed growth.

items.question: How do weeds affect crop production? Explain
items.answer:
Weeds are undesirable plants that affect crop production in
the following ways:

1. COMPETITION FOR WATER:
Weeds grow alongside crop plants in the same field. Their
roots spread in the same soil layer as crop roots and
absorb water meant for the crop. In times of water
scarcity (dry spells), this competition reduces the water
available to the crop, causing drought stress in crop
plants.
Example: Grass weeds growing in a wheat field absorb
water from the soil that should nourish wheat plants.

2. COMPETITION FOR NUTRIENTS:
Weeds absorb the same soil nutrients (nitrogen,
phosphorus, potassium) that crop plants need. Even if
the farmer adds manure and fertilisers, some of the
nutrients are taken by weeds instead of the crop.
This makes the crop deficient in nutrients and weak.

3. COMPETITION FOR SPACE AND LIGHT:
Weeds occupy physical space in the field, crowding out
crop plants. Tall weeds shade the crop plants, reducing
the amount of sunlight available for photosynthesis.
Without adequate sunlight, crops cannot produce enough
food and grow poorly.

4. INTERFERENCE IN HARVESTING:
Some weeds grow to similar heights as the crop and get
cut along with the crop during harvesting. Their seeds
or plant parts can contaminate the harvested grain,
reducing its quality and value.

5. POISONOUS WEEDS:
Some weeds are poisonous for animals and human beings.
If these weeds get mixed with fodder or food crops, they
can cause illness.

Due to all these harmful effects, removal of weeds (weeding)
is an essential agricultural practice that must be done at
the right time.

items.question: What precautions should a farmer take while
items.answer:
PRECAUTIONS WHILE USING WEEDICIDES:

1. COVER NOSE AND MOUTH: The farmer should always cover
his/her nose and mouth with a thick piece of cloth
during spraying. This prevents inhalation of the
chemical vapours.

2. COVER SKIN: The farmer should wear full-sleeved clothes
and, if possible, gloves to prevent the chemical from
coming in contact with the skin. Weedicides can cause
skin irritation or allergic reactions.

3. COVER EYES: Eyes should be protected with goggles or
the farmer should avoid spraying against the wind
direction to prevent chemicals from reaching the eyes.

4. SPRAY AT CORRECT TIME: Weedicides should be sprayed
during the VEGETATIVE GROWTH of weeds (before flowering
and seed formation) for maximum effectiveness. Spraying
at the right stage ensures weeds are killed before they
seed.

5. CORRECT DILUTION: Weedicides must be diluted with water
to the required concentration. Too concentrated can
damage the crop; too dilute will not be effective.

6. WASH AFTER USE: After spraying, the farmer should
thoroughly wash hands, face and other exposed body parts
with soap and water.

7. STORE SAFELY: Weedicide containers should be stored
away from food items and children.

WHY THESE PRECAUTIONS ARE NECESSARY:
Weedicides are powerful chemicals that can affect human
health. Prolonged exposure to these chemicals can cause
respiratory problems (breathing difficulties), skin
diseases, eye irritation and in extreme cases, more serious
health conditions. The farmer handles large quantities of
these chemicals during spraying, making protective measures
essential. Without these precautions, the farmer risks
serious health damage.

items.question: Write a detailed account of weeds, their
items.answer: WEEDS - DEFINITION, EFFECTS AND CONTROL METHODS

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
Weeds are undesirable, wild plants that grow naturally in
crop fields without being planted intentionally by the
farmer. They grow along with the crop and compete with it
for resources. The removal of weeds is called WEEDING.

HOW WEEDS APPEAR IN FIELDS:
- Weed seeds are naturally present in the soil from previous
seasons.
- Wind, water, birds and animals carry weed seeds from
outside into the field.
- Some weed seeds are accidentally mixed with crop seeds.
- Weeds grow rapidly, especially after rains and irrigation.

HARMFUL EFFECTS OF WEEDS:
1. COMPETITION FOR WATER: Weeds absorb water from the soil
meant for crop plants.
2. COMPETITION FOR NUTRIENTS: Weeds take up soil nutrients
(nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium) and fertilisers added
by the farmer.
3. COMPETITION FOR SPACE: Weeds occupy physical space in
the field, leaving less room for crop plants to spread
their roots and shoots.
4. COMPETITION FOR LIGHT: Tall weeds shade the crop, reducing
photosynthesis and food production.
5. INTERFERENCE IN HARVESTING: Some weeds grow to the same
height as the crop and get harvested along with it,
contaminating the produce.
6. POISONOUS EFFECT: Some weeds are poisonous for animals
and humans.
7. HOSTING PESTS AND DISEASES: Some weeds act as hosts for
pests and plant diseases that can spread to the main crop.

METHODS OF WEED CONTROL:

1. TILLING BEFORE SOWING (Preventive method):
Ploughing and tilling the field before sowing uproots
weeds. Exposed weeds dry up in sun and die. This is
done as part of soil preparation. Advantage: simple,
no additional cost.

2. MANUAL WEEDING (Physical method):
Physical removal of weeds by uprooting them or cutting
them close to the ground using a KHURPI. Done from time
to time as weeds grow. Seed drills can also uproot weeds.
Advantage: no chemicals, safe. Disadvantage: labour-
intensive, time-consuming for large fields.

3. CHEMICAL WEEDING (Weedicides):
Chemicals like 2,4-D are diluted and sprayed using a
sprayer. Most effective during vegetative growth stage
(before flowering and seed formation). Kills weeds
without damaging main crop.
Advantage: quick and effective for large fields.
Disadvantage: affects health of farmer if not careful;
may cause pollution if overused.

BEST PRACTICES FOR WEED CONTROL:
1. Remove weeds BEFORE they flower and produce seeds.
2. Combine tilling (at soil preparation stage), manual
removal (early crop stage) and weedicides (if necessary).
3. Take all health precautions while using weedicides.
4. Regular weeding is better than allowing weeds to grow
big - small weeds are easier to control.

Effective weed management ensures that the crop gets maximum
water, nutrients, space and light, leading to better yield
and quality produce.
